study_identification_part.si4_title: Comprehensive volumetric phenotyping of the neonatal brain in Down syndrome

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To conduct the first detailed regional volumetric analysis of the neonatal brain in Down syndrome by performing normative modeling of regional brain tissue volumes using a cross-sectional sample of 493 preterm- to term-born control neonates from the developing Human Connectome Project and quantifying deviation from the normative mean in 25 neonates with Down syndrome.

rci6_analysis_level.supporting_text: Motion-corrected and reconstructed T2-weighted images were corrected for bias-field inhomogeneities, brain extracted and segmented using the dHCP structural pipeline, an automated tissue structure segmentation algorithm optimized for the neonatal brain. T2-weighted images were segmented into seven main tissue/fluid classes: extra-cerebral cerebrospinal fluid (eCSF), lateral ventricles, cortical GM, WM, deep GM, cerebellum, and brainstem. Cortical GM, deep GM, and WM were further automatically segmented into the specific tissue segments listed in Table 1.

rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.answer: Motion correction (Cordero-Grande et al. 2018); Super-resolution reconstruction (Kuklisova-Murgasova et al. 2012); dHCP structural pipeline; Bias-field correction; Brain extraction; Automated segmentation (Makropoulos et al. 2014, 2016, 2018); Manual correction using ITK-SNAP v3.8.0
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The preprocessing pipeline is comprehensively described with references to the specific methods used at each step, including motion correction, super-resolution reconstruction, bias-field correction, brain extraction, automated segmentation using the dHCP structural pipeline, and manual quality control.
rci7_preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: Images were motion-corrected (Cordero-Grande et al. 2018) and super-resolution reconstructed (Kuklisova-Murgasova et al. 2012) resulting in a 0.5 mm³ isotropic pixel resolution. Motion-corrected and reconstructed T2-weighted images (Kuklisova-Murgasova et al. 2012; Cordero-Grande et al. 2018) were corrected for bias-field inhomogeneities, brain extracted and segmented using the dHCP structural pipeline (https://github.com/BioMedIA/dhcp-structural-pipeline), an automated tissue structure segmentation algorithm optimized for the neonatal brain (Makropoulos et al. 2014, 2016, 2018). Tissue segments for all DS and control scans were visually inspected for accuracy by the first author (A.F-G.), and where appropriate, any mislabelled voxels were manually corrected using ITK-SNAP (version 3.8.0) (Yushkevich et al. 2006).

rci8_quality_checking.detail: Neuroradiologist review with exclusion of acute infarction/parenchymal hemorrhage and major lesions in WM, cortical GM, cerebellum, or basal ganglia; minor common findings (<10 PWML, small subependymal cysts, small subdural hemorrhages, hemorrhages in caudothalamic notch) were not excluded; Visual inspection of all tissue segmentations by first author with manual correction of mislabelled voxels using ITK-SNAP v3.8.0; Exclusion criteria also included BSID-III cognitive and motor scores below 70 at 18 months for controls.
rci8_quality_checking.supporting_text: All MRI scans were examined by a neonatal neuroradiologist. Exclusion criteria for the dHCP scans were incidental findings with possible or likely significance for clinical outcome and/or imaging analysis, including acute infarction or parenchymal hemorrhage, and major lesions within the WM, cortical GM, cerebellum, or basal ganglia. However, we did not exclude neonates with < 10 punctate white matter lesions (PWML), small subependymal cysts, small subdural hemorrhages, or hemorrhages in the caudothalamic notch, as these are common findings in low-risk neonates (Carney et al. 2021). Exclusion criteria included incidental findings on MRI (Carney et al. 2021) and Bayley III Scales of Infant Development (BSID-III) cognitive and motor composite scores (test mean [SD]=100 [15]) below 70 (> 2 SD below the test mean) at 18 months. Tissue segments for all DS and control scans were visually inspected for accuracy by the first author (A.F-G.), and where appropriate, any mislabelled voxels were manually corrected using ITK-SNAP (version 3.8.0).

rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: Neonatal MRI data were acquired on a Philips Achieva 3 Tesla system using a dedicated 32-channel neonatal head coil and positioning system at the Evelina Newborn Imaging Centre, Evelina London Children's Hospital (UK) as per (Hughes et al. 2017). Data from 25 neonates with DS [12 female, 10 preterm births < 37 weeks GA, PMA at scan median (range) = 40.57 (32.43-45.57) weeks] (Table S1), scanned using the same acquisition parameters as dHCP controls, were used for analysis in this study.

nm4_response_variable.answer: Absolute and relative brain tissue volumes for: (1) Whole brain volumes (ICV, TBV, TTV); (2) Total GM or WM volumes (total cortical GM, total deep GM, total WM); (3) Regional volumes (total frontal lobe, total temporal lobe, total parietal lobe, total occipital lobe, total insula, total cingulate, posterior fossa, basal ganglia); (4) Specific tissue volumes (frontal/temporal/parietal/occipital/insula/cingulate GM and WM, cerebellum, brainstem, caudate nucleus, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, hippocampus, amygdala); (5) CSF-filled volumes (eCSF, lateral ventricles)
nm4_response_variable.reason: The response variables are comprehensively described in Table 1 of the paper, which lists all brain segments modeled. Both absolute volumes (in cm³) and relative volumes (as proportions of TTV, TBV, or ICV) were modeled.
nm4_response_variable.supporting_text: T2-weighted images were segmented into seven main tissue/fluid classes: extra-cerebral cerebrospinal fluid (eCSF), lateral ventricles, cortical GM, WM, deep GM, cerebellum, and brainstem (hereafter referred to as 'main tissue classes'). In this program, the eCSF included the third and fourth ventricles but excluded the lateral ventricles. The lateral ventricles included the cavum septum pellucidum, a transient fluid-filled cavity located in the midline of the brain, between the left and right anterior horns, which if still present, typically closes in the neonatal period. Cortical GM, deep GM, and WM were further automatically segmented into the specific tissue segments listed in Table 1. Tissue segments were used to extract absolute (in cm³) and relative (i.e. proportional) volumes.

caa1_clinical_dataset.answer: Early Brain Imaging in Down Syndrome (eBiDS) study and T21 study; Neonates with postnatally confirmed DS karyotype recruited from St Thomas' Hospital London; Scanned using same acquisition parameters as dHCP controls
caa1_clinical_dataset.reason: The clinical dataset is clearly described with study names, recruitment location, and confirmation that acquisition parameters matched the control cohort. The paper provides comprehensive details about the DS cohort including exclusion criteria.
caa1_clinical_dataset.supporting_text: Neonates with a postnatally confirmed karyotype for DS were recruited from the neonatal unit and postnatal wards at St Thomas' Hospital London and invited for a neonatal scan up to < 46 weeks PMA at scan. Additionally, former fetal scan participants with a confirmed postnatal diagnosis of DS were invited for a neonatal scan if they had consented to be contacted post-delivery. A total of 36 neonates with DS were recruited to the T21 and eBiDS studies between 2014 and 2021. Ten neonatal scans were excluded from analysis due to the use of old acquisition protocols, which were not in line with the dHCP controls. One neonate was excluded from analysis due to an acute brain infarction/parenchymal hemorrhage. Therefore, data from 25 neonates with DS [12 female, 10 preterm births < 37 weeks GA, PMA at scan median (range) = 40.57 (32.43-45.57) weeks] (Table S1), scanned using the same acquisition parameters as dHCP controls, were used for analysis in this study.

caa2_diseases_studied.reason: The disease studied is clearly identified as Down syndrome throughout the paper. The paper also describes the three mechanisms of DS: free trisomy 21 (nondisjunction, ~95%), translocation (~3%), and mosaicism (~2%).
caa2_diseases_studied.supporting_text: Down syndrome (DS) is the most common viable chromosomal abnormality affecting an estimated 1 in 700 ∼ 1000 live births worldwide annually. It is caused by the partial or complete triplication of Homo sapiens chromosome 21 (Hsa21), which can occur as a result of three different mechanisms: free trisomy 21 (i.e. a free supernumerary Hsa21 in all cells, also known as nondisjunction, in ∼ 95% of cases), translocation (i.e. translocation of all or part of Hsa21 onto another chromosome, in ∼ 3% of cases), or mosaicism (i.e. only a proportion of cells have trisomy 21, in ∼ 2% of cases).

caa6_deviation_metric.answer: Z-scores derived from GPR normative modeling; z-score = (observed - predicted) / predictive SD; Extreme deviations defined as z ≤ -2.6 or z ≥ +2.6 SD (representing top and bottom 0.5% of control population); Both absolute and relative volume z-scores computed
caa6_deviation_metric.reason: The deviation metric is clearly defined as z-scores normalized by the predictive confidence (standard deviation) from the GPR model. The threshold for extreme deviations is explicitly stated as ±2.6 SD.
caa6_deviation_metric.supporting_text: The difference between predicted and observed values, normalized by the predictive confidence (i.e. standard deviation, SD), represents the deviation of a data point from the expected mean, expressed as a z-score in units of SD (Marquand et al. 2016). Subsequently, the GPR model was used to extract individualized absolute and relative volume z-scores (by segment, as listed in Table 1) for an independent sample of 25 neonates with DS, accounting for sex, PMA at scan (in weeks), and age from birth (in weeks) variables. Extreme deviations in volume were taken as a z-score ≤ -2.6 or ≥ +2.6 SD, representing the top and bottom 0.5% of the control population, as per (Dimitrova et al. 2021).

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Group-level comparisons: Mann-Whitney U test and Kruskal-Wallis one-way test of variance for DS vs control and DS CHD+ vs CHD- comparisons; Effect sizes assessed using Cliff's delta (categorized as negligible d≤0.147, small 0.148≤d≤0.33, medium 0.34≤d≤0.474, large d≥0.475); Age-related analyses: Simple linear regressions of volumetric z-scores vs PMA at scan with median regression (Tau=0.5) and quartile regressions (Tau=0.25, 0.75) using quantreg package; Goodness of fit assessed with R² and adjusted R²; Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (Rho) for correlation strength; Extra sum-of-squares F-test to compare slope and intercept parameters between groups; WBV covariation analysis: Linear and median regressions of volumetric z-scores vs WBV z-scores with WBV-adjusted group median z-scores derived via median regression; Akaike information criterion (AIC) for model comparison; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction for multiple comparisons (pFDR<0.05 for significance)
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Neonates with DS showed significantly reduced whole brain, cerebral white matter, and cerebellar volumes in absolute terms; in relative terms, enlarged cortical GM with reduced WM, disproportionately enlarged deep GM (particularly lentiform nuclei and thalami), reduced relative frontal/cingulate/insular/occipital lobes with enlarged temporal/parietal lobes, severely reduced cerebellum, and enlarged lateral ventricles and eCSF; age-related deviation patterns suggested progressive divergence from controls with advancing PMA for several structures; CHD+ neonates showed greater volumetric reductions than CHD- in select regions by later ages.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Absolute volumes: DS neonates had significantly smaller WBV (ICV median z=-1.05, TTV z=-1.76, large effect sizes d=-0.50 to -0.76, pFDR<0.0001); most tissue segments were significantly smaller except lentiform nuclei (z=-0.03, ns) and eCSF (z=+0.27, ns); lateral ventricles were enlarged (z=+1.05, d=+0.52, pFDR<0.0001); total WM (z=-1.91, d=-0.80) was more deviated than cortical GM (z=-1.22, d=-0.59); cerebellum was markedly reduced (z=-2.43, d=-0.93). Relative volumes: total cortical GM enlarged (z=+1.37, d=+0.46, pFDR=0.0001), total WM reduced (z=-0.59, d=-0.32, pFDR=0.012); lentiform nuclei disproportionately enlarged (z=+2.23, d=+0.82, pFDR<0.0001); thalami enlarged (z=+1.50, d=+0.59); temporal and parietal lobes enlarged (z=+0.64 to +2.03, d=+0.43 to +0.86) while frontal, cingulate, insular, occipital lobes reduced (z=-0.71 to -1.57, d=-0.36 to -0.66); cerebellum severely reduced (z=-1.83, d=-0.85); lateral ventricles markedly enlarged (z=+1.98, d=+0.78); eCSF enlarged (z=+1.11, d=+0.51). Age effects: WBVs showed gradual deviation with advancing PMA (negative slopes significantly different from control for ICV, TTV); cerebellum showed pronounced age-related deviation with 12 neonates at extreme z≤-2.6; eCSF excessive in preterm scans (z>+2) decreasing by term; lateral ventricles consistently enlarged across ages. CHD impact: CHD+ vs CHD- showed significant slope difference for occipital WM (F=18.21, pFDR=0.0084) with strong negative correlation in CHD+ (ρ=-0.89, R²=0.78); trends for greater WBV reduction and regional tissue deficits in CHD+ by later ages, potentially linked to low oxygen saturation and complex cardiac defects.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: This study provides the first comprehensive volumetric phenotyping of the neonatal brain in DS using normative modeling. The authors note that while not immediately clinically applicable, the ability to assess phenotypic severity at the neonatal stage may help guide early interventions and ultimately improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. Individual z-scores allow quantification of deviation severity and identification of neonates with extreme deviations (z≤-2.6 or ≥+2.6). The finding that CHD may contribute to additional brain volumetric changes beyond baseline DS phenotype has important implications for early monitoring and intervention in this high-risk subgroup. Future work should focus on linking neonatal brain phenotypes to later neurodevelopmental outcomes, testing associations with cognitive, motor, and behavioral measures, and developing stratification tools for personalized intervention planning.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: Small DS sample size (n=25) limits statistical power, particularly for subgroup analyses (CHD+: n=13, CHD-: n=12); Single-site, single-scanner study limits generalizability; Cross-sectional design prevents assessment of longitudinal trajectories; Narrow age window (32-46 weeks PMA) does not capture fetal or later developmental periods; No normative model validation metrics reported (no cross-validation, held-out test set, or external validation); Cannot separately assess contribution of cavum septum pellucidum to lateral ventricular volume or 3rd/4th ventricles to eCSF; Multiple comorbidities in DS cohort (CHD in 52%, GI issues in 32%) complicate interpretation; No neurodevelopmental outcome data for DS cohort to assess clinical predictive value; Manual segmentation corrections needed despite automated pipeline; Need for larger, multi-site, longitudinal studies with validation cohorts

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: Methodological details: Segmentation included cavum septum pellucidum within lateral ventricles (could not be assessed separately); eCSF included 3rd and 4th ventricles (also could not be assessed separately); relative volumes calculated as proportion of TTV for most structures, except lateral ventricles (proportion of TBV) and eCSF (proportion of ICV); left and right regions were consolidated. DS characteristics: 52% (13/25) had congenital heart defects (CHD), most commonly AVSD; 32% (8/25) had GI malformations; multiple clinical comorbidities common (see Supplementary Tables S2-S3). Data availability: dHCP data from third release (2021) available at http://data.developingconnectome.org; eBiDS data available from corresponding author upon reasonable request. Statistical approach: Non-parametric tests used due to non-normal distributions; Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction applied throughout; multiple regression approaches (simple linear, median, quartile) used to assess robustness. Quality control: One DS neonate excluded due to acute brain infarction/hemorrhage; 10 DS neonates excluded due to old acquisition protocols not matching dHCP; controls excluded if BSID-III scores <70 at 18 months or significant MRI findings. Lentiform nuclei were the only structure showing no deviation from controls in both absolute volume and age trajectory (slope F=0.03, pFDR=0.86; intercept F=0.54, pFDR=0.49). Twelve neonates (48%) showed extreme cerebellar deviations (z≤-2.6). Four neonates showed extreme WBV reductions (TTV z≤-2.6), three of whom had multiple cardiac defects and low oxygen saturation at scan.
